A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AnyBimanual and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary Sections 6–9. The retained material and additions can be reliably matched.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations on 12 simulated and nine real-world tasks, component ablations, and supplementary experiments with five demonstrations per real-world task.

after.justification: V2 reports revised simulation results, retains the original real-world experiments, and adds qualitative examples and an empirical decomposability analysis.

M1.justification: Section 7.2 revises the specified skill-manager transformer from hidden size 128 with four attention heads to size 256 with eight heads. This is a limited reported architectural revision; skill scheduling, visual alignment, and training losses remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether this reflects retraining or correction of the specification.

E1.justification: The principal training and evaluation task suites remain unchanged. Figures 15–17 add a bimanual 'put item in drawer' case to the qualitative and decomposability analyses; v1 included this task among unimanual pretraining tasks, without the corresponding bimanual evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains RVT-LF, PerAct-LF, PerAct2, the pretraining control, and the same AnyBimanual variants. Component-ablation membership and the PerAct2 rollout comparison also remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 and Table 1 increase the reported simulation evaluation budget from 25 to 100 episodes per task, retaining the 20/100-demonstration training budgets and success criterion. Section 7.2 revises transformer dimensions, and Section 8.5 introduces an entropy-based diagnostic analysis. These are bounded changes within the existing evaluation framework.

E4.justification: New Figures 15–16 examine skill scheduling and visual masking in additional examples. Section 8.5 and Figure 17 examine whether skill-weight entropy tracks decomposition difficulty and task success across four tasks. Existing component ablations, skill clustering, failure cases, and limited-data experiments are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 17 newly reports a fitted logarithmic relationship and a correlation statistic labeled r = 0.934. Neither version reports training-seed variability or confidence intervals. The increased number of evaluation episodes is a sampling change, not evidence of additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 extensively replace simulation and ablation results. The reported 100-demonstration mean for PerAct plus AnyBimanual changes from 21.67% to 32.00%, while PerAct2 changes from 9.00% to 14.67%. These are results under revised reported settings, not demonstrated same-setting improvements. Figures 15–17 add findings; real-world Tables 3 and 7 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations (1)–(6) are unchanged. The new entropy analysis is an empirical heuristic, without a new formal derivation, theorem, proof, or guarantee.

C1.justification: The abstract revises its quantitative simulation-superiority claim from a 12.67-point to a 17.33-point success-rate margin. The central contributions—transferring unimanual policies through skill scheduling and visual alignment—and the reported 84.62% real-world success remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 8.5 newly interprets higher skill-weight entropy as indicating greater decomposition difficulty and presents its relationship with success as an applicability diagnostic. The existing cross-embodiment and zero-shot generalization limitations, along with the failure-mode explanations, are retained.

D1.justification: New Section 7.3 explicitly identifies the skill primitives as CLIP embeddings of unimanual instruction templates, clarifying an existing initialization mechanism. Section 7.2 revises the transformer configuration. Hardware, the principal training recipe, Table 6, and the planned code-release statement remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The same 73 references and substantive positioning relative to foundation policies, skill learning, and bimanual manipulation are retained. Changed citation back-reference pages reflect document reflow.

P1.justification: V2 makes limited wording edits and adds short subsections on skill primitives, visualization, and decomposability, renumbering subsequent appendix subsections. The main narrative and section organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figures 15–17, adjusts the introductory and pipeline illustrations, and moves Figure 2 earlier. Existing tables retain their structure, while surrounding text and appendix material reflow. This is a limited presentation extension rather than a comprehensive redesign.

improvement.justification: Reporting 100 rather than 25 simulation episodes per task strengthens empirical sampling, while the added mechanism visualizations and primitive-initialization explanation improve interpretability and reproducibility. These gains are limited by reporting problems: Section 4.2 reverses the RVT-LF and PerAct-LF average-result attributions, and the new entropy analysis lacks detailed protocol information. Higher headline scores alone do not establish improvement because the reported settings changed.
